say: Welcome back, inquirers! Today our numbers get BIG: all the way up to 100 000. That is more than the number of people who fit in the National Stadium.
Big numbers are often rounded. Today we find out what a rounded number can hide, and we solve riddles about 5-digit numbers. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Draw five boxes on your whiteboard: ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. I turn over one digit card at a time. Write it in a box straight away. No moving it later!
Round 1: make the biggest number. Round 2: make the number closest to 50 000. Where will you put a 4? A 5?
You have the cards 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9. How many of the numbers you can make will round to 50 000 to the nearest thousand? Write your guess.
stuck: Stuck: which ten thousands digit could give a number near 50 000? There is no 5 0 … because there is no 0 card.
Not sure about one number: draw a number line from 49 000 to 50 000. Where is the halfway mark?
Finished early: which number you can make is closest to 70 000?

say: “36 482 to the nearest thousand. It is between 36 000 and 37 000. Halfway is 36 500. 36 482 is just below halfway, so it is nearer 36 000.”
“A number rounds to 25 000. The smallest it could be is 24 500, because 24 500 is exactly halfway and halfway rounds up. The largest is 25 499. 25 500 would round up to 26 000.”
“7 × 3 089. I round 3 089 to 3 000, so the estimate is 21 000. I rounded DOWN, so the real answer must be a bit more: 21 623.”

do: Ask: “Which two round numbers is it between? Where is the halfway mark?”
Ask: “Could the number be bigger than that and still round to the same number?”
Ask: “Which clue gives you the fewest numbers to try? Start there.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Draw a number line. Mark the two round numbers and halfway.”
Hint 2: “Look only at the digit to the right of the place you round to.”
Hint 3: “For odd or even, choose the ones digit FIRST.”

say: “Siti says 49 999 rounds to 50 000 to the nearest 10, 100 AND 1000. Is she right?”
“Ravi says 45 000 rounds to 40 000 to the nearest ten thousand. Is he right?”
ask: “Siti says 49 999 rounds to 50 000 to the nearest 10, 100 AND 1000. Is she right?”
Siti is right: 49 999 is only 1 away from 50 000, so it rounds to 50 000 every time. Ravi is wrong: 45 000 is exactly halfway between 40 000 and 50 000, and halfway rounds up, so it rounds to 50 000.

say: “Today you used number lines to round, and you worked backwards to find what a rounded number could really be.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l2-title.note: Objective: Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 using a number line, work backwards from a rounded number to find the smallest and largest possible numbers, use rounding to estimate and check, and solve 5-digit number riddles, digit-card puzzles and number patterns. Thinking strategies taught today: DRAW A NUMBER LINE, WORK BACKWARDS, MAKE A LIST IN ORDER and USE THE CLUES ONE AT A TIME. Materials: Digit cards 0 to 9 (one set per child), mini whiteboards, a place-value chart (ten thousands to ones), a blank number line strip. Online: children cut out paper digit cards before the lesson and move them on camera; the tutor marks the number lines on the slides. Time plan: opening 0 to 1, sneak-peek puzzles 1 to 4 (two ideas we have not learnt yet; answers shown to the tutor only, on camera, nobody marked), warm-up game 4 to 6 (one short round), quick questions 6 to 8, explore 8 to 18 (a Go further what-if is on the slide from minute 8), teaching 18 to 30 (click to reveal each step and answer; the "your turn" slides are optional, skip them if short of time), brain break 30 to 34, worksheet page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 34 to 50 and check together 50 to 53, short teaching before page 2 53 to 58, worksheet page 2 (on your own) 58 to 76 and check together 76 to 80, talk time 80 to 85, exit ticket 85 to 88, looking back (reflection) 88 to 90 (2 minutes). After question 3 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children).

p4l2-check.note: Minutes 1 to 4 (3 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. About 90 seconds each. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and held to the camera at the same moment for everyone (or shown only to you on camera). Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards up in front of the group, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Ask for volunteers first if you want a reason said aloud; nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) Nearer to 7 000. 7 200 is only 200 from 7 000 but 800 from 8 000, and it is left of the halfway dot 7 500. 2) 7 500 and 8 499. The real number is from 7 500 to 8 499 (7 499 rounds down to 7 000; 8 500 rounds up to 9 000). A GOOD REASON: Find the two round numbers and the halfway mark. Halfway or more rounds up. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. After question 3 on page 1 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l2-warm1.note: Minutes 4 to 6 (one short round, about 2 minutes: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Place It Right with 5 digits. Children draw five boxes: TTh, Th, H, T, O. Shuffle digit cards 0 to 9 and turn over one at a time (online: hold it up to the camera). After EACH card, children write it in one empty box at once and cannot move it. After five cards, read the numbers aloud: biggest wins. Round 2: closest to 50 000 wins. Click to show the thinking question. Talk: "A 4 or a 5 in the ten thousands place. If you have a 4, you want the other digits BIG (49 9..). If you have a 5, you want them small (50 1..)." 49 999 is 1 away and 50 100 is 100 away. Listen for children who compare the distances; that is rounding thinking, and it comes straight back in the explore.

p4l2-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Read each aloud, whiteboards up together, then click. After 2: watch for 6045 or 600 045; say it as "60 thousand, 0 hundreds, 4 tens, 5 ones". After 3: the thousands digit was 9, so the ten thousands digit changes too. After 4: the 0 holds the hundreds place. After 5: 36 815 is between 36 000 and 37 000; ask "Is it nearer 36 000 or 37 000?" Do not teach the halfway rule yet. Answers: 7000, 60 045, 60 600, 43 058, 37 000.

p4l2-explore1.note: Minutes 8 to 13. Pairs work with digit cards 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9 (online: paper cards on camera). Ask for a prediction first: how many numbers will round to 50 000? Let them try numbers freely at first. Common first try: 52 479 (rounds to 52 000) or 54 279 (54 000). Push them towards numbers starting with 4 9. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: which number you can make is closest to 70 000? (72 459, which is 2459 away: there is no 6 card, so nothing can start 69.) GO FURTHER (on the slide from minute 8, so nobody waits): Which number you can make is closest to 70 000? Why can you not make 70 000? Answer: 72 459 (2 459 away). 70 000 needs a 0 card and there is none; with the cards 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9 the closest below is 59 742 (10 258 away).

p4l2-explore2.note: Minutes 13 to 18. Let pairs keep working, then gather. Collect numbers on the board and test each one together. Answers: 1) 49 527, 49 572, 49 725, 49 752. 2) A number that rounds to 50 000 must be from 49 500 to 50 499. With no 0 card, nothing starts 50, so it must start 49, and the hundreds digit must be 5 or 7 (2 and 4 are too small). Each of those gives 2 numbers. 3) 49 752, only 248 away. The next slides teach the halfway mark properly.

p4l2-we1.note: Teach. Clicks: halfway line, the number, then the steps. Think-aloud: "Which two thousands is 36 482 between? 36 000 and 37 000. The halfway mark is 36 500. My number is 18 short of halfway, so it is nearer 36 000." Then the shortcut: "Look only at the digit just to the right of the place I round to: for thousands, the hundreds digit. 4 is less than 5, so round down." Ask: "What about exactly 36 500?" (halfway rounds UP: 37 000). The sign ≈ on the last line means "is about"; say so if children have not met it.

p4l2-try1.note: Whiteboards. a) Between 58 300 and 58 400; halfway 58 350; 58 361 is past it. b) Between 58 000 and 59 000; halfway 58 500; 58 361 is before it. c) Between 29 900 and 30 000; halfway 29 950; 29 960 is past it, so 30 000. Watch for 29 000 or 291 00: the 9 hundreds becomes 10 hundreds, which is another thousand.

p4l2-we2.note: Work backwards from the rounded number. Ask first: "Could the number be 25 600? 24 400? 25 500?" Let children argue, then click the band. Think-aloud: "Everything from the halfway mark below, 24 500, up to just before the halfway mark above rounds to 25 000. 25 500 itself is halfway, and halfway rounds up, to 26 000. So the largest whole number is 25 499." Common mistake: saying 25 500 is the largest.

p4l2-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) Halfway below 7000 is 6500. b) Halfway above 40 000 is 40 500, so 40 499. c) 795, 796, … 804: count them, 10 numbers. Many children say 9 or 11: list them to check.

p4l2-we4.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (two rounding clues together: an optional stretch example, not on the worksheet any more). Click the yellow band (clue 2), then the blue band (clue 1). Ask: "Which numbers are in BOTH bands?" Check one at the edge: 4250 rounds to 4250 to the nearest 10, but to 4300 to the nearest 100, so it is out. 4244 rounds to 4240, so it is out too.

p4l2-we3.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 estimates and checks). Draw the bar: 7 equal parts. Think-aloud: "3089 is close to 3000. 7 × 3 thousands = 21 thousands. I rounded each part down by 89, so my estimate is too small, and the real answer is more." Work out 7 × 3089 together in columns if time (21 623). Ask: "If the number were 2950, would the exact answer be more or less than 21 000?" (less: 2950 was rounded up).

p4l2-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Forgetting to carry when the digit to change is a 9 (63 950 to the nearest hundred written as 63 900 instead of 64 000). (2) Working backwards with the wrong limits: saying the largest number that rounds to 63 000 is 63 500 instead of 63 499. (3) Digit-card puzzles: putting 0 in the ten thousands place, or making the biggest number first and hoping it is even, instead of choosing the ones digit first.

p4l2-break.note: Four minutes. Call numbers such as 34 999, 25 000, 47 210, 15 500, 44 999. Online: children hold up 1 to 5 fingers for the ten thousand they point to. Ask after 25 000: "It is exactly halfway. Which way?" (up, to 30 000).

p4l2-ws1.note: Minutes 34 to 50. Walk around. Ask "Which two round numbers is it between? Where is halfway?" before giving any help. Q1: 63 950 to the nearest 100 and 9049 to the nearest 10 are the traps. Q2b: write 5340, 5341, 5342 … and check each one on the number line. CHOOSING: after question 3 every child may carry on or try the Think harder page. Invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l2-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1: 63 950 is halfway between 63 900 and 64 000, and halfway rounds up. 80 503 to the nearest 1000: 503 is past 500, so 81 000. Q2b: halfway is 5345, so 5345 rounds up to 5350; 5354 rounds to 5350 but 5355 rounds up to 5360. That is 10 numbers. (Two clues together, 5350 to 5354, is a Think harder question in the question bank.) Q3c: 6 × 4982 = 29 892, only 108 less than the estimate.

p4l2-teachriddle.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4a starts with a rounding clue). Use the clues one at a time: the rounding clue turns a huge list into a short range. Ask after step 1: "Which numbers between 19 500 and 20 499 could have digits that add to only 5?" Check at the end: 20 003 rounds to 20 000; 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 3 = 5; ones digit 3. For Q4b ("find ALL"), remind them: list in order, starting with the smallest ten thousands digit.

p4l2-teachpattern.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). Row 1: 36 000 − 34 800 = 1200, 37 200 − 36 000 = 1200: add 1200. Row 2: take away 1250. Row 3: add 2500: 48 500 is not above 50 000 yet, the next one, 51 000, is. Ask: "Is 50 000 in this pattern?" (no). Watch for children who cross a ten thousand wrongly: 37 200 + 1200 = 38 400.

p4l2-teachcards.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Think-aloud for step 1: "Odd means the ones digit is odd. I decide that FIRST, then put the biggest of the rest in front." Step 2: "Smallest: the smallest digit that is not 0 goes first, then 0. The ones digit must be even, and the only even card left is 4." Step 3: compare the best number on each side of 50 000. Ask: "Why not 4 … something?" (we need a 9 in the thousands to get close: 49 720).

p4l2-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially anyone who still rounds 63 950 to 63 900. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q4a, Q5 and Q6a first. The other parts are a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which.

p4l2-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4a: 47 500 to 48 499 with hundreds digit 6 means 47 6..; ones digit 1 and tens digit double that (2) gives 47 621. Q4b: ten thousands digit 1 leaves 1 more in 4 places (4 numbers), ten thousands digit 2 leaves 0 (20 000). Q5c: 99 990 + 10 = 100 000. Q6b: odd means 3 or 5 last; smallest is 3 first and 5 last: 30 685. Q6c: 58 630 is 1370 away; 60 358 is 358 away.

p4l2-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 55 555 (66 666 rounds to 70 000; 44 444 rounds to 40 000). 2) 69 741 (259 away; the closest number above 70 000 is 71 469, which is 1469 away). 3) Add 2250 each time: 24 000, 26 250. 4) 100 (from 3450 to 3549).

p4l2-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q7. Answers: 1) 15 (10 starting with 1, 4 starting with 2, and 30 000). 2) 40 004, which is 11 km more.

p4l2-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: For Q1, what can the ten thousands digit be? For each choice, how much is left to share among the other four places? For Q2, if the number starts with 39, how must it end? Is there a palindrome 39 _ 93 bigger than 39 993? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l2-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: list in order by the first digit so nothing is missed. The 6 ways for two 1s (in two of the four places Th, H, T, O): 11 100, 11 010, 11 001, 10 110, 10 101, 10 011. The 4 ways for a 2: 12 000, 10 200, 10 020, 10 002. Q2: count on from 39 993 to 40 000 (7) and on to 40 004 (4): 11 km.

p4l2-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 85. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: Siti is right: 49 999 is only 1 away from 50 000, so it rounds to 50 000 each time (49 999 → 50 000 to the nearest 10 because 9 ones round up). Ravi is wrong: 45 000 is exactly halfway between 40 000 and 50 000, and halfway rounds up, to 50 000. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake.

p4l2-exit.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Answer: 75 000 (652 is past halfway). The smallest whole number that rounds to 74 000 is 73 500. Extension: how many whole numbers round to 45 000 to the nearest thousand AND to 50 000 to the nearest ten thousand? (500: from 45 000 to 45 499.)

p4l2-reflect.note: Minutes 88 to 90 (2 minutes). LOOKING BACK. Children fill in the box on the Investigation page, the page every child has (something I did well; the hardest part was; what helped me; one thing I could try next). Say: "You can write, tick or pass. Ticking I am still stuck is a good thing to do: it tells me where to help." Model one yourself first: "Something I did well: I drew the number line. The hardest part was working out which way a number like 450 rounds. What helped me: marking the halfway point on the number line. One thing I could try next: a number line for every rounding question." Do not ask anyone to read theirs out. If a child wants to share, take one volunteer and thank them for the strategy. Never grade it, never correct it, never collect it for marks and never show it to the group. You may look at a child's page only when the child holds it to your camera. Never ask for photos or private messages. If I am still stuck is ticked, check in during the open session: a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never send a DM. Praise strategies ("you drew it", "you asked for help"), not speed or scores.
